Annual Report 


Young Men’s Christian Association of Montreal 
For the Year Ending April 30th, 1923 


Characteristics of Period: 


If I were asked to characterize the past year in the life of our 
Young Men’s Christian Association, I would say that it has been a year 
marked by a return to normalcy. The period of depression and defla- 
tion which began in 1920, due to changing economic conditions, has 
undoubtedly been passed and we have had a return to more stable con- 
ditions. 

So far as quality and quantity of work done, this last year has 
set a new standard and there are abundant evidences in the lives of 
young men and boys which testify that the guiding principles of this 
Movement have not misled us, and that the self-sacrifice of those who 
make the work possible has not been in vain. 


Membership. 


The total membership in good standing on April 30th was 5,143, 
being an increase of 90 during the period under review. 
The report by Branches is as follows: 


Boys Men Total Total Total 
1922-23 1921-22 1920-21

1,562 3,562 5,124 5,034 5,131 


Increases are observed in Westmount and North Branches and 
among the boys in the West End Branch near St. Henri. 


3 


Some of the best minds in our organization to-day are urging that 
a re-organization of our membership records be made with a view to dis- 
covering those who are not necessarily privilege users of our buildings 
but who have joined a spiritual movement and desire to have a share in 
reaching its central objective. 


The Boards of Management of each Branch should take early 
steps to correct the past errors in membership philosophy and make clear 
the present confusion as to who are the field and who are our force. Our 
records should show those who are members of a brotherhood of Christian 
men working for men of all lands, and it is these men who should operate 
our great buildings as one of the processes of developing Christian 
character. 


Whatever form and phraseology admission to the Association 
may in the future assume, entering this movement as a member should 
involve four things:— 


(a) BELIEF IN THE ENTERPRISE—Belief in, and desire to see ac- 
complished, those Christian purposes that lie at the heart of the Associ- 
ation. 


(b) WILLINGNESS AND DESIRE TO TAKE PART IN OUR COMMON 
TASK, each according and in proportion to his abilities and talents. 
What is meant here is active participation in the work of some committee 
or group. This work would be for some men continuous and organized, 
and for others informal and occasional. 


(c) AN ANNUAL CONTRIBUTION TO THE BUDGET OF THE ASSOCI- 
ATION for the support and promotion of the movement, voluntary as to 
the amount; a gift varying in size according to one’s interest and ability. 


(d) MEMBERSHIP IN SOME PROTESTANT EVANGELICAL CHURCH. 


The most hopeful element in the present membership situation 
is the general recognition of our danger and the determination to keep 
ever in the forefront of our thinking the fellowship or movement aspects 
of our work. 


Among the events which have contributed to the strengthening 
of this spirit may be mentioned the following: Conference at Macdonald 
College in September; week-end training camp for boys at Dorval Island; 
luncheon to Sir Herbert Ames, Financial Secretary, League of Nations, 
and former President of our Association; foreign work meetings; financial 
campaigns; golf matches at Senneville and Mount Bruno. 


Finance. 


The policy of rigid economy in the administration of our work put 
into effect two years ago, was continued throughout the past year and 
we have found it possible to continue the work in all our branches. 


~The Treasurer’s statement will show a total income of $292,024.30 
and an expenditure of $295,797.11 as compared with $317,177.99 and 
$317,106.24 in 1921-22. The receipts from subscriptions for all branches 
and the National Council totalled only $59,646.20 as compared with 
$67,298.97 last year and $100,907.21 two years ago. 


4 


We are obliged to record a deficit of $3,376.58 on our year’s 
operations. 


The major reason for this excess of expenditure over income is the 
shrinkage in the revenues of some of our branches and their inability to 
curtail expenditures. Another reason is the loss from our ‘‘Civic Mem- 
bership” list of a number of generous subscribers, some by death, others 
through circumstances or business changes. We are glad to report, 
however, that new names have been added so that the net reduction in 
the number of ‘Civic Members” is six. 


While the principal cause for our deficit is due to our Branches, 
we must add a less active interest in this side of our work on the part of 
Board and Committee members. The merit of our cause is unquestioned 
and we can at once go forward to a much greater work if the lay forces 
of the Association will rally to this great opportunity. May we never 
forget the power of example and the effect of success or failure in this 
great city on weaker Associations in less privileged centres. 


Our system of accounting and financing from one central office 
has now been in operation two years and continues to justify the wisdom 
of making this change and has proved to be of great value to our entire 
organization. 


Our mortgage indebtedness which originally stood at $70,000.00 
but which had been reduced to $60,000.00 prior to this year, was further 
reduced to $46,500.00 by the use of funds received from the G.T.R. in 
connection with the purchase of the Point St. Charles building. 


We gratefully acknowledge the receipt of a bequest from the late 
Theo. J. Labatt of $2,500.00. Your Directors are impressed with the 
importance of creating an endowment fund and again call to the attention 
of Association friends the statilizing effect which this would have upon 
our work. 


With the successful conclusion of the effort to secure four million 
dollars to care for the accrued liability, the Retirement Fund for Em- 
ployed Officers was launched last July, and our veteran and much 
beloved Secretary, Mr. D. A. Budge, formally retired from professional 
service in the Association after rounding out a wonderfully rich experience 
of 48 years and ten months. Your Board welcomed this opportunity, and 
did themselves the honor, of electing him as a Director of the Association 
and a member of the Finance Committee. 


The Building Branches: 


As the activities of the Central, North, Westmount and Railroad 
branches have been very fully reviewed in the reports presented recently 
to their Annual Meetings, and through the columns of the press, it is 
unnecessary to refer to them again at this time. 

The three first named buildings have been occupied now for eleven 
years and are rendering invaluable service to the community where they 
are operating. They have all been well maintained, but have already 
reached the limit of their capacity particularly in the North End and 
in the Educational and Dormitory sections of the Central Building. 

May we express here our conviction that no generation in the 
history of the city has had such complete provision for its social, mental, 


5 


spiritual and physical needs as is made by these buildings. Men come 
to them because of an opportuniy to belong to a good club whose fees 
are within their ability to pay, to satisfy personal tastes and realize worthy 
ambitions. From such humble things as a meal and a bath up to the 
great values of health education, friendship and inspiration, almost all 
the normal needs of men can be met in the buildings of the Montreal 
Y.M.C.A. This, of course, accounts for thousands of the men and boys in 
our membership, from the working boy in the night school to the business 
man in the noon-day gym class. As Mr. Paul Super says, ‘““‘What an 
asset for helpfulness! What a field for service! Are we not proud 
that these magnificient institutions are Christian possessions? Indeed 
what else but Christ in the minds and hearts and purses of men could 
have produced these buildings and their work ?” 


The Non-building or Community Branches: 


Important studies in Chicago and elsewhere indicate that the 
capacity of an Association building to serve a community is limited to 
an aréa of one mile radius. Natural or artificial barriers, such as a wide 
river, canals, or large railroad yards, still further restrict the service as 
the currents of traffic and intercourse are broken by these obstacles. 
It is only the most earnest and energetic who go long distances, or over 
real difficulties, to secure the institutional benefits of the Association. 

Recognizing this principle, your Directors have continued the 
most valuable work being done by the branches in Cote St. Paul, Verdun 
Maisonneuve, St. Henri, and the district just east of Bleury Street. In 
each of these densely populated areas there are thousands of young men 
and boys who are desperately in need of the services of the brotherhood 
and the ideal of the fourfold life. 

It is impossible here to give any adequate picture of the work done 
in the above sections. but the following summary from the annual report 
of the Verdun Branch will convince the most skeptical of the large field 
of usefulness this type of Association can fill in any community under 
competent leadership: 

—School Boys’ Service Group organized with 4 members has 
grown to 70. 

—High School Club organized, meeting in ‘Y’ weekly. 

—Library of 422 volumes is very popular and is meeting a great 
need. No Public Library in Verdun at present. 

—Community singing and motion pictures on the pier attended 
by 2,500 people. 

—Community singing for six months at the Grand Trunk Railway 
Shops, with a weekly average attendance of over 600 men. 

—Hockey and skating rink had a fine season. Masquerades and 
carnivals attended by over 1,200 children. 

—Twelve hockey teams competed in leagues. 

—Four hundred boys from soccer leagues of Cote St. Paul, 
Verdun and Point St. Charles attended rally in church and heard address 
on ‘“‘Sportmanship.” 

—Twenty-six boys attended Association night school in Verdun. 

—Stay-in-School campaign in co-operation with parents and press 
an outstanding success. 

—Physical work for Boys’ Clubs from all churches carried on in 
gym of High School two evenings per week. 


6 


—Pathfinder Bible Class, with average attendance of 22, led by 
“Y’ Secretary. 

—Debating Club of 20 serious-minded young men trained in 
Art of Public Speaking and Debate. 

—Y’ motion picture entertainments given in Anglican, Methodist, 
and Presbyterian Churches, Verdun Schools, ‘500’ Club, and Sons of 
England. 

—Twenty-two boys attended Kamp Kanawana. 

—Innumerable personal interviews held on most vital matters 
with boys, young men, and parents. 

—Groups using Y.M.C.A. office included I1.0.D.E., Baby Welfare 
Association, Boy Scouts, Verdun War Memorial Committee, LaSalle 
A.C., Verdun Hockey Club. 

—In all, 544 boys and 240 young men were in organized activi- 
ties. 

—Many thousands attended mass activities, such as School 
athletic meets, masquerades, community sing-songs, Vacation Bible 
Schools, motion picture shows, etc. 

This summary of work done under the leadership and direction of 
one Secretary from a small office on Church Avenue, Verdun, is but ty- 
pical of Branches in other districts referred to in this section of this report. 


Summer Camps. 


Thirty years ago, when out-door camps for boys were first estab- 
lished, some good men and women held up their hands in holy terror! 
The boys would get their feet wet! They would be exposed to the 
“night air’? which everybody knew was deadly posion! They were quite 
sure that sleeping in ‘‘draughty’’ tents would kill the boys, or, at least, 
they would be returned to their homes as invalids. Camping was an 
innovation in those days. To-day it is recognized as one of the golden 
opportunities for reaching young men and boys with a character-building 
programme, and it is estimated that over 800,000 boys were in summer 
camps last year. The sturdy values which come from meeting nature on 
her own ground are well evidenced in the abounding health and natural- 
ness of our lads at Kanawana. 

The Camp is a veritable godsend to the boys employed in factory 
and office. They are like plants and trees and must have fresh air 
and sunshine if they are to thrive and grow. 

The enrolment last year was as follows:—

Audited and Certified Correct. 


P. S. ROSS & SONS, 


Chartered Accountants. 


Montreal, May 19th, 1923. 


The completed hospital has contributed largely to the speedy recovery 
of those who were ill. 

CAMP OTOREKE, for young men, was operated for three weeks, 
with 36 campers in attendance. Thirty-eight boys from Kanawana were 
also at the Camp for brief periods of time while on hikes. The programme 
and esprit de corps were excellent. 


Cavalry Camps. 


During the month of June last year, we provided Y.M.C.A, 
services to those men of the cavalry units in training at St. Johns. 


Military Hospital Work. 


For nearly a year we have been carrying on a service of motion 
pictures to the men in hospitals at both St. Agathe and St. Anne’s, which 
has been deeply appreciated by officers and men. The cost of this 
service has been borne by our National Council. 


Our greatest undertaking. 


The year has been marked by a square facing of the problem of 
winning to an allegiance to our Lord and His Church, a new generation 
of young men. 

One year ago we attended a conference at Lakehurst, N.J., where 
for several days over one hundred employed officers of the North Ameri- 
can Associations tried to evolve a plan whereby the City Associations 
would more adequately realize the central purpose of their work. 

It was generally recognized that the Boys’ and Student Depart- 
ments had gone far ahead of the rest of the movement in confronting 
their members with the Living Christ, and that at all costs the City 
Associations must formulate plans for coming into more vital contact 
with these young men in the late teens and all through the twenties. 

Dr. Mott consented to set aside his other duties and, at great 
personal sacrifice, devote four months of his time to giving leadership 
to this undertaking which was to be supplemented by teams of men 
visiting other cities. 

The tour was launched in our own city on November 28th, when 
in six sessions over sixteen hundred men heard his messages. These 
groups included business and professional men, McGill student 
body, working forces of the branches, ninety clergymen of all denomina- 
tions, the Association employed officers, and 250 older boys and young 
men. 

Dr. Mott spoke with deep earnestness and conviction, and those 
who have followed closely the fall and winter programme in all our 
branches, will bear testimony to the great values these meetings were to 
our entire work. The results were unusually fine in our North Branch. 

The addresses delivered on this tour are being published in book 
form, and in a few weeks will be on sale in our Central Branch library. 

The Week of Prayer was again observed in the month of Novem- 
ber. The booklet prepared by Dr. Fosdick was of great value and ran 
through six editions before the demand for it was filled. 


12 


The Training Centre. 


Among the fruitful ideas that have gripped City Association 
leaders during the last few years, few have gained more widespread 
acceptance than the conviction that the Association should be a training 
centre for the entire staff. 

This desire has been increasingly possible to act upon, due to a 
growing literature on training, the appearance of courses of study and our 
proximity to McGill University and its affiliated colleges. 

A beginning was made along these lines two years ago, and im- 
mense strides were taken during the year that has gone. Fifteen of our 
employed officers attended the Wednesday morning sessions at Divinity 
Hall and the Wesleyan College, and we gratefully acknowledge the con- 
tribution which Drs. S. P. Rose and E. M. Best of the Theological 
Colleges have made to this vital matter of training. The former led a 
course in ‘“The Content of the Gospels” and the latter in ‘‘The Theory 
of the Y.M.C.A.”’ 

Two of our staff completed Summer School Courses at Lake 
Couchiching—one of the enterprises conducted by the National Council— 
Mr. F. O, Stredder, in Boys’ Work, and Mr. P. Long, in Physical Edu- 
cation. 

Several men were recruited during the year for Christian callings— 
two of them, members of our Railroad Branch, for the Association 
Secretaryship. 


International Convention. 


Another milestone in our International history was passed last 
November when the 41st International Convention was held in Atlantic 
City. 

Over 1,500 voting delegates were in attendance, and Montreal 
was represented by 17 men, four of them being from the Westmount 
Junior Board. 

The gathering was highly inspirational in character, and notable 
addresses were delivered by :— 

Dr. Richard Roberts. 
Dr. Robert E. Speer. 
Dr. Harry E. Fosdick. 
Dr. John R. Mott. 
Mr. Robt. P. Wilder. 

The report of the International Committee read like a chapter 
from the Book of the Acts, and was a remarkable summary of the World 
Work of the Movement. 

Four important Commission presented reports as follows:— 

(1) The Occupation of the Field. 

(2) The Approach to the Churches. 

(3) Standing Commission on Associations. 
(4) Convention Rules and Representation. 

The findings of these Commission have since been considered by 
your Directors in relation to our own work. 

A radical step was taken in authorizing the calling together of the 
first Constitutional Convention, which will convene next October in 
Cleveland. It is quite possible that this Legislative Assembly will re- 


13 


place the great Triennial Conventions which have been largely 
inspirational and not legislative. 


National Work. 


Montreal has often been referred to as standing at the ‘““Gateway 
of Canada” and it is a constant source of pride to all our citizens that 
our outlook is truly national and not parochial. 

The leadership of this city in point of finance, ocean and railroad 
transportation, industry and population is unquestioned. It is but 
natural, therefore, that as an Association—the first founded on this 
Continent—we should gladly accept a large share of the responsibility 
for the National Council, which is the agency charged with the super- 
vision and entension of our organization in Canada. We should also 
remind ourselves that the Montreal group were largely responsible for 
bringing the National Council into being in the City of Winnipeg some 
twelve years ago. 

The National Council was charged with the huge task of serving 
Canada’s sons in the recent Great War. To them, in any emergency, 
this and all other Canadian Associations must look for guidance. The 
record of their progress during the year which has gone is, therefore, of 
the deepest interest to us. 

There is no object in obscuring the fact that in common with other 
agencies, the Y.M.C.A. in Western Canada has been most severly tested. 
The devotion of small groups of Christian men in some of the Western 
cities to our cause borders on the heroic. It would appear as if the 
condition there in places parallels the years following the Civil War in 
the United States when the Y.M.C.A. passed through its most trying 
times. 

The operating deficit of the National Council at the close of their 
fiscal year was $12,000.00, a situation which we should view with real 
concern. 

Two Associations in Canada were closed last year, viz., Paris and 
Sault Ste. Marie. Two new ones were, however, opened in Kitchener 
and Windsor, and a new Railroad Building is in course of construction 
at Sioux Lookout. 

Seven other cities have requested the National Council to help 
establish Associations in order that the needs of boys and young men 
might be more adequately met. 

Our contribution to the finances of our National work last year 
totalled $10,000.00 toward their budget of about $60,000.00. 


World-wide Extension. 


We have always felt a moral and spiritual obligation to extend 
our work into unoccupied centres in non-Christian lands as well as in 
Canada. Our stewardship of methods, money, men and ideals has ever 
been recognized by the large-hearted and broad-minded men of this 
movement. 

For over seventy years Association men in this city have demon- 
strated the principles and methods underlying successful work for young 
men: the very year that David McConaughy left to pioneer the work 


14 


in India, we assumed responsibility for his budget: one family placed his 
name on the payroll of their company and have continued this support 
until the present time; Montreal provided funds for the first building 
in the White House Campaign for 30 buildings to be erected through the 
world at a cost of one million dollars; many of the men who are leading 
this organization in Canada and throughout the world received their 
training in this city! Truly a recognition of our obligation to others! 

In view of this past achievement, it is encouraging to report 
another successful year in helping finance International or Foreign work. 
The funds secured were as follows:—

We have had as speakers during the year the following Association 
Secretaries from foreign fields :— 

Dr. A. C. Hart, General Secretary, Jerusalem. 
Mr. Fletcher S. Brockman, China. 

Mr. Cornelius, Rural Dept., India. 

Mr. Ghose, Publications, India. 

Mr. J. D. Paul, India. 

Mr. Geo. A. Gregg, Seoul, Korea. 

Mr. Hugh Cynn, Seoul, Korea. 

Mr. Scott, Valparaiso, Chili. 

It is with a feeling of pride that we record the departure from our 
midst of one of our own Westmount boys, in Mr. E. Bruce Copland, who 
is now in China with the Presbyterian Church. His career in the Far 
East will be followed by us all with prayerfull interest. 

While the results of last year are of very great encouragement to 
us all we must keep vividly before us the limitless stretches still unoc- 
cupied throughout the world. For example, we have occupied but one 
city in Korea, and twenty more urge our entrance. In five of the great 
Provinces of China, with an average population greater than the whole 
Dominion, we have no Association. When we recall that the Native 
Secretaries now in the countries already entered outnumber the 
Canadian and American by three to one, there is great hope for the future. 
Dr. Mott has pointed out that, ‘‘The need of the world is an index to 
the Will of God. Not Fear, but Faith, points the road on which to 
move forward.” 


Obituary. 


We mourn the loss by death during the year of Mr. George E. 
Williams, formerly a member of our Metropolitan Board; Mr. J. H. Mc- 
Keown, of our Westmount Board; Mr. A. G. Mitchell, of our Railroad 
Board, and Mr. Harcourt Farmer of the Teaching Staff of our Central 
Branch. These men gave of themselves unsparingly in Association 
service and held a large place in our love and esteem.

Conclusion. 


As one reviews the work of the Association for the past year, and 
the extent and variety of our service is considered, it re-eemphasizes and 
accentuates the fact that notwithstanding the growing interest by lunch- 
eon clubs and other organizations in certain types of work for boys, the 
Y.M.C.A. is actually touching literally and vitally thousands of boys 
and young men of all classes and groups including the sub-normal and 
underprivileged, and is giving them an opportunity for a true expression 
of life whereby they may reach a fuller and more useful manhood. 

The encouragement and re-assurance than comes from an analysis 
of the year’s results is found in the truth that in spite of the two years of 
depression and deflation through which we have passed, and the conse- 
quent difficulty facing many young men in earning a livelihood, we have 
been able to maintain a strong and aggressive programme—city-wide, 
nation-wide, and world-wide—which has continued to merit the confi- 
dence and receive the endorsement and necessary financial support of 
the large-hearted and forward-looking corporations and citizens of this 
first city of Canada. 

With returning prosperity the coming year should register an 
even higher mark in efficiency and further advances in our service. 

We desire to extend our sincere and grateful thanks and apprecia- 
tion to all those who have so faithfully and unselfishly labored together | 
with us in the work, and more especially to members of Boards throughout 
the city. Without their aid little could have been accomplished. To 
obtain larger results we need even more sacrificial effort on the part of 
our present workers, and our hope is that a much larger number of volun- 
teer laymen may give of their time and thought and prayer during the 
year upon which we have already entered. 


In the words of Emerson: 


“And thou shall succor men, 
’Tis nobleness to serve; 

Help those who cannot help again, 
Beware from Truth to swerve.” 


Respectfully submitted, 


General Secretary.
